growth_story.headline: Tonga's income per person is at a record high after a lost 2000s, but the gains rest on remittances, aid and rebuilding while people keep leaving.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2002 Tonga's income per person grew 2.2 percent a year, the tail of a long stretch the World Bank credits to stable government and steady spending on health, education and infrastructure. From 2003 to 2010 it shrank by 1.2 percent a year: a long civil service strike ended in a large pay deal in 2005, riots damaged the capital in November 2006, and the 2009 global recession cut remittances from abroad. Income per person fell from 4,051 constant dollars in 2002 to 3,631 in 2009 and did not pass its 2002 level again until 2014. Since 2011 growth has averaged 2.1 percent a year, and 1.8 percent over 2016 to 2025 against 0.7 in the decade before, so that in 2025 income per person reached its highest level yet, 4,934 dollars. The sources tie this recovery mostly to remittances and foreign aid rather than to gains in productivity, and to rebuilding after repeated cyclones and the 2022 volcanic eruption and tsunami, which together with COVID-19 cut income per person by 1.7 percent in 2022.

threads.title: Stable early decades
threads.text: The World Bank describes fast growth from the 1970s to the mid-1990s, built on stable government and steady spending on health, education and infrastructure. A slowdown after the 1990s then eroded those early gains, and growth over 1990 to 2002 averaged 2.2 percent a year.

threads.title: Unrest, then a global slump
threads.text: In the mid-2000s a long civil service strike ended in a large pay rise, and in November 2006 riots over political reform caused heavy damage in the capital, Nuku'alofa. As recovery began, the 2009 global recession cut remittances from the United States and New Zealand, and income per person fell 5.3 percent that year.

since_last_year.text: In November 2025 the IMF reported that rebuilding, strong remittances, a tourism rebound and larger-than-expected grants drove growth in fiscal 2025, and it expected growth to slow as reconstruction winds down. The data show income per person up 3.2 percent in 2025, to a new high. In July 2026 the World Bank found that growth over the past decade came mainly from money flowing in from abroad rather than from higher productivity at home.

growth_story.tension: The data show income per person at its highest level ever in 2025 and growth of 2.1 percent a year since 2011, while the sources describe stalled convergence, weak productivity and slow long-term growth. Part of the gap is people: the population peaked in 2012 and then fell as Tongans emigrated, so income per person can rise faster than the economy as a whole. The sources also tie recent growth to remittances, aid and rebuilding rather than to stronger production at home.
